newsitem.title: JAPAN: ADB sidesteps N. Korea and Russia issue.
newsitem.headline: ADB sidesteps N. Korea and Russia issue.

text.p: The hottest topic at the Asian Development Bank meeting which began on Sunday was not on the agenda, was not discussed and the subjects were not even there.
But applications by North Korea and Russia to join the ADB were the focus of discussion behind the scenes at the bank's 30th anniversary gathering, delegates said.
Bank membership, sought after by poor nations seeking an economic shot in the arm, was not on the agenda because annual meetings do not take up specific topics, ADB officials said.
Neither North Korea nor Russia was invited to Fukuoka, although both has openly expressed their desire for membership.
Key players in the back room bargaining in this southern Japanese city were Japan, the United States, South Korea and China.
Japan, standing tall as top donor to the bank and host of the meeting, nevertheless kept the lowest of profiles on the membership issue.
"We need to consider it carefully," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters. "We must take into account judgement of our diplomatic authorities, and consult with other nations."
Speculation is rife that Japan, which has no diplomatic ties with the Stalinist state, has blocked Pyongyang's inclusion into the ADB under pressure from its Foreign Ministry.
Tokyo alleges North Korean agents abducted Japanese citizens in the past and has been reluctant to give even food aid to North Korea.

Although Japanese officials denied the speculation as "complete garbage", Mitsuzuka's reference to "diplomatic authorities" was widely seen as proof that his ministry is mindful of the Foreign Ministry's caution over the issue.
In contrast, South Korea has made no secret of its support for an ADB with North Korea as member.
"We support it. We expect North Korea's entry will lead to stability in the Korean peninsula and the world," Yong-Keun Lee, Korea's temporary alternate governor to the bank, told Reuters.
He said it would open up North Korea and "they will realise that a central planned economy is inferior to a market economy."
Lee said China also was in favour of North Korea membership while the United States is said to be reserving a decision.
The Russian situation may be even more complicated.
"Geographically, one side (of Russia) is Europe and the other is Asia," Lee said.
Although the United Nation's Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific has recognised Russia as an Asian country, some members are sceptical about its Asian standing.
Others questioned the role of Russia within the ADB.
"Will it be a borrower or a donor?" said Toyoo Gyohten, chairman of the Institute of International Finance and a former Japanese finance ministry official.

The weight that is likely to be thrown around by a country like Russia may be disruptive to the tightly-run bank, which has just 12 members on the board of governors and two key voting shareholders -- Japan and the U.S. -- with 13.2 percent each.
Voting shares are allocated in proportion to the shares held in the bank and a Russian entry may tip the balance of power within the bank, Lee said.
